note: There were no continuous front lines: shaded areas show ground held by the French and their allies, or by the coalition, and arrows show campaigns, all approximate.

chapters.title: The invasion camp and Trafalgar
arrows: Villeneuve's combined fleet sails from Ferrol to Cádiz
The Grande Armée leaves the Channel camps for the Rhine
The combined fleet sails out of Cádiz
Nelson's fleet attacks in two columns
chapters.text: When Britain declared war in May 1803, Napoleon camped an army along the Channel coast around Boulogne to invade England, but first his fleets had to win control of the Channel. In August 1805 Admiral Villeneuve's French and Spanish fleet turned south from Ferrol to Cádiz instead of sailing for Brest, and on 27 August the army left its camps and marched for the Rhine to fight Austria. On 21 October Nelson's fleet attacked the combined fleet off Cape Trafalgar and captured or destroyed most of it, ending any threat of invasion.

chapters.title: Ulm and Austerlitz
arrows: Lannes and Murat: Rhine to Wertingen
Ney's corps closes on Ulm from the north
Soult crosses the Danube at Donauwörth to Augsburg
French pursuit down the Danube to Vienna
Kutuzov's Russians fall back to Olmütz
French advance from Vienna into Moravia
chapters.text: On 9 September 1805 an Austrian army crossed into Bavaria, France's ally, and took up position around Ulm. Napoleon's corps crossed the Rhine in late September, swung round behind it to the Danube and trapped it, and General Mack surrendered at Ulm on 20 October. The French marched down the Danube, took Vienna in mid-November and followed the Russians into Moravia, where on 2 December Napoleon beat the Russian and Austrian armies at Austerlitz. Austria made peace at Pressburg on 26 December.

chapters.title: Jena–Auerstedt and the fall of Prussia
arrows: Right column: Soult and Ney through Hof
Centre: Bernadotte and Davout through Schleiz to Naumburg and Auerstedt
Left: Lannes and Augereau through Saalfeld to Jena
chapters.text: Prussia, with Saxony, went to war in October 1806 before its Russian ally could arrive. Napoleon's army came through the Thuringian Forest in three columns and on 14 October beat the Prussians twice in one day, at Jena and, under Marshal Davout, at Auerstedt. Erfurt surrendered on 16 October, Napoleon entered Berlin on 27 October and Stettin gave in without a fight; Blücher's last field force was cornered at Lübeck on 6–7 November, and Magdeburg capitulated days later.

chapters.title: Poland, Eylau, Friedland and Tilsit
arrows: Davout and Murat to Posen and Warsaw
Ney and Soult to Thorn and the Vistula
Napoleon to Heilsberg, Friedland and Tilsit
chapters.text: The French pushed on into Prussian Poland, taking Warsaw on 28 November 1806 and crossing the Vistula, but a Russian army now stood in their way. A winter battle in the snow at Eylau on 7–8 February 1807 left both sides shattered, and the French went into winter quarters while they besieged Danzig, which fell on 24 May. In June Napoleon advanced again, crushed the Russians at Friedland on 14 June and reached the Niemen; at Tilsit in July Russia made peace and Prussia lost half its lands.

chapters.title: Portugal occupied, Spain rises
arrows: Castaños and Reding trap Dupont at Bailén
Wellesley lands and advances to Vimeiro
Moore's advance and retreat to Corunna
chapters.text: To close Portugal to British trade, Junot's army marched through allied Spain and occupied Lisbon on 30 November 1807. In early 1808 French troops seized Spanish fortresses and entered Madrid, and when Napoleon made his brother Joseph king, Spain rose in revolt: at Bailén in July a whole French corps surrendered, the French abandoned Madrid and fell back to the Ebro, and a British army under Wellesley won at Vimeiro and forced them out of Portugal. Napoleon came himself in November, retook Burgos and Madrid and chased Sir John Moore's British army to Corunna, and Zaragoza fell after a terrible siege in February 1809. In May Wellesley drove Marshal Soult out of Porto.

chapters.title: Aspern-Essling and Wagram
arrows: Austrian retreat through Bohemia to the Marchfeld
French advance down the Danube to Vienna
Crossing at Aspern-Essling, thrown back to Lobau
chapters.text: In April 1809 Austria struck again, invading Bavaria while much of the French army was in Spain. Napoleon hurried back, beat the Austrians in five days of fighting around Abensberg and Eckmühl, and marched down the Danube to take Vienna on 13 May. His first attempt to cross the river was thrown back at Aspern-Essling (21–22 May), a rare defeat for Napoleon in person, but in July he crossed from the island of Lobau and won the huge battle of Wagram (5–6 July). Austria agreed an armistice at Znaim on 12 July.

chapters.title: Talavera and the Lines of Torres Vedras
arrows: Wellesley advances up the Tagus to Talavera
chapters.text: Wellesley (soon Lord Wellington) advanced into Spain and fought the French at Talavera on 27–28 July 1809, but had to fall back towards Portugal. In 1810 the French overran Andalusia and besieged the Spanish government in Cádiz, and Marshal Masséna invaded Portugal, taking Ciudad Rodrigo and Almeida; Wellington checked him at Bussaco, then withdrew behind the Lines of Torres Vedras, forts he had built across the hills north of Lisbon. Masséna's starving army wintered around Santarém and retreated to Spain in March 1811, while Soult took Badajoz; after the battles of Fuentes de Oñoro and Albuera in May the allies held all of Portugal again.

chapters.title: Ciudad Rodrigo, Badajoz and Salamanca
chapters.text: In January 1812, while Napoleon prepared to invade Russia, Wellington stormed the border fortresses of Ciudad Rodrigo (19 January) and Badajoz (6 April). He then advanced into Spain, took Salamanca and on 22 July routed Marshal Marmont's army near the city; King Joseph abandoned Madrid, Wellington entered it on 12 August, and Soult had to give up the siege of Cádiz and all of Andalusia. But Wellington failed to take the castle of Burgos, and as French armies converged he retreated to Portugal in November, leaving Madrid and Salamanca to the French again.

chapters.title: The march on Moscow
arrows: The Grande Armée crosses the Niemen to Vilna
Barclay's First Army retreats to Smolensk
Bagration's Second Army retreats to Smolensk
Kutuzov withdraws through Moscow to Tarutino
chapters.text: On 24 June 1812 Napoleon crossed the Niemen into Russia with more than 450,000 men. The Russian armies retreated rather than fight, and the French took Vilna on 28 June, Minsk on 8 July and Vitebsk in late July, then stormed Smolensk in mid-August. At Borodino on 7 September Kutuzov's army stood and fought, in what is often called the bloodiest single day of the war, and then withdrew; Napoleon entered a nearly empty Moscow on 14 September, which soon burned, while Kutuzov camped to the south at Tarutino.

chapters.title: The retreat from Moscow
arrows: Retreat along the Smolensk road to the Berezina
From the Berezina back to the Niemen
Chichagov advances to Minsk and Borisov
chapters.text: No peace offer came, and on 19 October the French left Moscow. Blocked at Maloyaroslavets, Napoleon had to retreat along the ravaged road by which he had come, harassed by Kutuzov's army and by Cossacks; Vyazma was lost on 3 November, Polotsk and Vitebsk on the northern flank, and then Smolensk as frost set in. Russian armies closed in on the Berezina, where the remnants escaped across hastily built bridges on 26–29 November at a terrible cost, and the last of them recrossed the Niemen at Kovno on 14 December.

chapters.title: Germany 1813: Lützen to Leipzig
arrows: Wittgenstein through Berlin to the Elbe
Blücher crosses the Elbe and closes on Leipzig
chapters.text: After the disaster in Russia, Prussia changed sides in February–March 1813, and Russian and Prussian troops reached Berlin, Hamburg and Dresden. Napoleon raised a new army, won at Lützen (2 May) and Bautzen (20–21 May), retook Dresden and pushed into Silesia before an armistice in June, and Davout recaptured Hamburg. When fighting resumed in August, with Austria and Sweden now in the coalition, Napoleon won at Dresden but his marshals were beaten at Grossbeeren, the Katzbach, Kulm and Dennewitz, and at Leipzig, the 'Battle of the Nations' (16–19 October), the allied armies defeated him and drove him back to the Rhine.

chapters.title: Vitoria, the Pyrenees and Toulouse
arrows: Orthez and the march on Toulouse
chapters.text: In May 1813 Wellington's British, Portuguese and Spanish army advanced across northern Spain, outflanking each French position; the French blew up Burgos castle, and on 21 June Wellington broke King Joseph's army at Vitoria. The French gave up Valencia and Aragon and fell back over the Pyrenees, a counter-attack by Marshal Soult towards Pamplona was beaten off in late July, and San Sebastián (8 September) and Pamplona (31 October) fell. Wellington then crossed into France, won at the Nivelle and at Orthez, sent troops into Bordeaux, and on 10 April 1814 attacked Soult at Toulouse, not knowing that Napoleon had already abdicated.

chapters.title: The invasion of France
arrows: Schwarzenberg crosses the Rhine at Basel
Blücher crosses the Rhine and marches on Nancy
Napoleon's Six Days: Champaubert to Vauchamps
Montereau: Schwarzenberg thrown back to Troyes
Blücher turns north to the Aisne
chapters.text: In late December 1813 and on 1 January 1814 the allied armies crossed the Rhine into France, while others freed the Netherlands. Heavily outnumbered, Napoleon fought brilliantly: after a defeat at La Rothière he beat Blücher's columns in the Six Days' campaign (10–14 February) and drove Schwarzenberg back to Troyes. But Blücher held on at Laon (9–10 March), and when Napoleon marched east to cut the allies' communications they marched straight on Paris, which capitulated after a battle on 30 March; the allies entered the city on 31 March, and Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau on 6 April.

chapters.title: The Hundred Days and Waterloo
arrows: Napoleon's march from Golfe-Juan to Paris
Napoleon crosses the Sambre to Ligny
Grouchy pursues the Prussians to Wavre
Prussians attack at Plancenoit and pursue
chapters.text: Napoleon escaped from Elba, landed near Antibes on 1 March 1815 and marched on Paris, which he reached on 20 March as Louis XVIII fled. On 15 June he crossed into the Netherlands at Charleroi, and on 16 June beat the Prussians at Ligny while Marshal Ney held Wellington at Quatre Bras. On 18 June Wellington's army held its ridge south of Waterloo until Blücher's Prussians, who had rallied at Wavre, arrived on the French flank, and the French army broke. Napoleon abdicated again on 22 June, and the allies entered Paris on 7 July.

baseYears.why: the 1807–1813 border data draws occupied Prussia and Poland (1807–08), most of Spain (1809–11) and Lithuania and the road to Moscow (1812) inside the French Empire; 1806 borders keep Prussia, Spain and Russia whole so the occupied areas can show who held what (the Duchy of Warsaw and Westphalia are therefore not drawn as separate states)
the 1814 border data already shows France after the first abdication (Paris lies in a shape labelled Grand Duchy of Berg), so the 1813 borders are used for the invasion of France
